lead: Malware is short for malicious software: any program written to damage a system, steal from it, or take control of it. Every family name — virus, worm, trojan — answers one question: what does this code need in order to run and reach the next machine? A virus needs a host file and usually a user who opens it. A worm needs only a network. A trojan needs a user's trust, because the user installs it on purpose. The family name drives real decisions: what a signature can catch, what one patch can stop, and what only user habit can prevent.
prereq: Read 1.3 for threat, vulnerability and exposure; malware usually enters through an unpatched service.

sections.h3: Classify by what the code needs

blocks.text: Malware spreads by one of three routes, and the route gives the family its name.

items: Needs a host file plus a user action → virus.
Needs a user who trusts it → trojan.

blocks.text: The payload is the harmful job the code does: delete files, encrypt them, open a remote shell. The vector is how it arrives: an email attachment, a pirated installer, a USB stick, an unpatched network service an attacker scans (see 1.4).
The family name says nothing about the damage. A quiet trojan that opens a backdoor can cost a bank far more than a noisy virus that garbles a few files.

sections.h3: Virus: a host file and a user's hand

blocks.text: A virus is code attached to another program or file, called the host. It runs when the host runs. It cannot travel alone: something must carry the infected file to a new machine, and a user or the operating system must open it. Common subtypes:

items: Boot sector virus: infects the first sector of a disk and runs before the operating system loads.
Macro virus: written in a document's macro language, so it travels inside a word-processor or spreadsheet file and runs when the document opens.
Polymorphic virus: rewrites its own bytes on every copy, often encrypting the body with a fresh key, so a fixed byte signature no longer matches.
Stealth virus: hides its change by intercepting the operating system's read of the file and returning the clean original.

blocks.text: A virus needs both a host to live in and a trigger to start. That is why attachments, shared drives and pirated software remain lasting vectors: each one asks a person to click.

sections.h3: Worm: the network is the host

blocks.text: A worm is standalone code. It copies itself across a network through a service on the target machine, with no host file and no user action. It finds victims by scanning address ranges and trying the same exploit on each.

The Morris worm of 1988 was the first to get wide public attention. No user opened anything: it used a bug in the mail program, a bug in another network service, and a list of common weak passwords. Every success produced a new machine running the same code.

This changes defence. A worm offers one door to close: patch the service it exploits and the outbreak stops, even on machines whose users do nothing. A virus of the same speed still waits for people to open a file, so patching the network changes nothing.

A trojan is a program the user installs on purpose because it looks useful — a video codec, a game crack, a free system cleaner — with something else inside. It does not copy itself; the attacker or the user moves it. The payload is whatever the author chose:

items: Backdoor: keeps a hidden login or remote shell open for the attacker (see 1.7).
Rootkit: hides files, processes and open ports from the operating system's own tools.
Logic bomb: stays silent until a programmed condition is met — a date, a missing file, a login name.
Ransomware: encrypts files and demands payment, often by UPI or cryptocurrency.

blocks.text: Most malware, whatever the family, moves through the same five stages:

items: Delivery: the code reaches the machine (attachment, download, network service).
Persistence: it arranges to run again after a reboot — a registry run key on Windows, a cron entry or systemd unit on Linux.
Propagation: it spreads to further machines; a trojan may skip this step entirely.

blocks.text: The program flaw a worm exploits — a buffer overflow, a missing input check — is separate from the malware that uses it. Fixing such flaws is the subject of Unit 6.

figure.caption: All three families sit under one root because they are sorted by what they need, not by damage. The virus branch still needs a host file and a user; the worm branch needs only the network.

spec.aria: A tree with Malware at the root and virus, worm and trojan as branches, showing that a virus needs a host file, a worm spreads alone, and a trojan hides in a useful program.

examples.question: A worm doubles the number of infected machines every 10 minutes. It starts with 1 infected machine at 09:00. (a) How many machines are infected at 09:10, 09:20 and 09:30? (b) How many at 10:00? (c) Between which two doubling steps does the count pass 1,00,000 machines, and at what clock times? (d) Why does patching one bug stop this outbreak, while a virus with the same doubling time would not be stopped by one patch?
steps: Each 10-minute interval multiplies the count by 2, so after k intervals N = 2^k, starting from 1 machine.
09:10 is k = 1, giving 2 machines; 09:20 gives 2² = 4; 09:30 gives 2³ = 8.
09:00 to 10:00 is 60 minutes, so k = 60 ÷ 10 = 6 and N = 2⁶ = 64 machines.
Step 16: 2¹⁶ = 65,536 machines at 09:00 + 160 min = 11:40. Step 17: 2¹⁷ = 1,31,072 at 11:50. Since 65,536 < 1,00,000 < 1,31,072, the mark is crossed between 11:40 and 11:50.

(d) A worm needs no user action, so every reachable unpatched machine is a victim and one patch closes the only door. A virus with the same speed would still need 64 users to open the infected file by 10:00, so the network patch alone would not stop it.
examples.answer: 2, 4 and 8 machines at the first three steps; 64 machines at 10:00; the 1,00,000 mark is passed between step 16 at 11:40 (65,536 machines) and step 17 at 11:50 (1,31,072 machines).

examples.question: Same worm, but the number of infected machines triples every 10 minutes, starting from 1 machine at 09:00. How many machines at 09:30, and after how many intervals does the count first exceed 1,00,000?
steps: After k intervals N = 3^k, from 1 machine.
3¹⁰ = 59,049 and 3¹¹ = 1,77,147. Since 59,049 < 1,00,000 < 1,77,147, the count first exceeds 1,00,000 at k = 11 intervals, that is at 09:00 + 110 min = 10:50.
examples.answer: 27 machines at 09:30; the count first exceeds 1,00,000 after 11 intervals, at 10:50, with 1,77,147 machines.

traps: Calling every piece of bad software a virus. If it spreads alone over the network it is a worm; if it hides inside a program the user wanted, it is a trojan.
Saying a worm infects files. A worm is standalone code; it may drop files, but it does not need a host file to spread.
Assuming a logic bomb runs on a timer. It runs on any programmed condition — a date, a file deletion, a login name.
Forgetting that a trojan can have zero propagation. A trojan that only opens a backdoor never spreads by itself.

quiz.q: Define malware and name the three families when malware is sorted by how it spreads.
quiz.a: Malware is software written to damage, spy on, or take control of a system. Sorted by spread: virus (needs a host file and usually a user action), worm (spreads by itself over a network), trojan (hidden inside a program the user installs on purpose).

quiz.q: Why does a signature-based scanner catch a simple file infector but often miss a polymorphic virus?
quiz.a: A signature is a fixed pattern of bytes taken from known malware. A file infector copies the same bytes into every host, so the pattern matches. A polymorphic virus rewrites its own bytes on each copy, so the stored pattern no longer appears. A stealth virus keeps its bytes but hides its change from the operating system's file read.

quiz.q: A worm infects 1 machine at 08:00 and doubles every 15 minutes. How many machines are infected at 09:00?
quiz.a: 08:00 to 09:00 is 60 minutes, so k = 60 ÷ 15 = 4 intervals. N = 2⁴ = 16 machines.

quiz.q: A user downloads a free PDF converter. Two days later the machine accepts logins from an unknown foreign IP address, and no other machine on the network is affected. Name the family and the payload, and justify both.
quiz.a: Family: trojan — the user installed it deliberately and it did not spread, so there is no self-propagation. Payload: backdoor — a hidden remote login was left open. A worm is ruled out by the absence of spread; a virus is ruled out because no host file was infected and no other user opened anything.

quiz.q: Why does patching a single network service stop a worm outbreak but not a macro virus outbreak?
quiz.a: The worm reaches every machine through that one service with no user action, so closing the service removes its only entry point. A macro virus arrives inside documents that users open, so it needs no service; the defence there is user behaviour and document scanning.

quiz.q: List the five stages of the malware lifecycle in order.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry malware analysis splits into static analysis (examining the bytes without running them) and dynamic analysis (running the sample in a sandbox and watching files, registry and network traffic). Analysts write detection rules such as YARA patterns that describe a whole family, and map behaviour to frameworks such as MITRE ATT&CK. Ransomware is now sold as a service, with separate specialists for access, encryption and money movement.
